In the UK, the communications regulator mandates that the World Cup be listed as a "Listed Sporting Event," meaning in theory all World Cup matches must be broadcast free-to-air, while broadcasters BBC and ITV do not air advertisements during the cooling break. China's National Radio and Television Administration stipulates that broadcasting rights for the World Cup, Asian Games and Olympics must be monopolised by CCTV, which at the last minute acquired this edition's broadcasting rights from FIFA at a low price in recent years.

PCCW wins broadcasting rights for third consecutive term; per capita cost ranks among the world's highest

Back in Hong Kong, PCCW, which holds licences for both free and pay TV as well as fixed-line and mobile telecommunications, has secured the broadcasting rights for three consecutive editions. Conversely, after TVB suffered losses following its World Cup broadcast and Cable TV ceased pay-TV operations, no remaining bidder in the market possesses cross-platform and bundling advantages.

FIFA is believed to have sized up PCCW's "cord-cutting" pressure on customer retention and thus charged Hong Kong a certain broadcasting fee. The exclusive Hong Kong broadcasting rights for this World Cup are reported to have been concluded at HK$170 million, a sum slightly lower than before, yet on a per capita basis Hong Kong still ranks among the world's highest. Although the price of a "pass" to watch World Cup matches has not increased this edition, and restaurants and eateries have joined in screening broadcasts, with "online football commentary fever" giving fans more choices, the days of a "universally shared" World Cup remain far off.

Commercial sponsorship shapes the rules of the game — far more than just "watching the match and incidentally checking out the boots"

During the World Cup, from pitch-side advertising to Video Assistant Referees (VAR), everything represents a golden opportunity to capture audience attention — it is hardly surprising that commercial sponsorship and licensing constitute another important revenue stream for FIFA. FIFA divides sponsors into four main tiers, and sponsors worldwide also implicitly compete for global influence every four years.

In recent editions, the stable top-tier FIFA partners have all been globally renowned brands, including Adidas, Coca-Cola, Hyundai and Visa. Partners also include potential host nations — for instance, Qatar Airways has been a sponsor since 2017, while Saudi Aramco, the oil company of Saudi Arabia (host of the 2034 World Cup), is also sponsoring this edition, in an open transaction with FIFA.

Chinese sponsors, which in recent editions gained attention through Chinese-language advertising slogans, have seen their sponsorship value for this edition drop by nearly 70%. Wanda, a top-tier partner in the previous two editions, was removed for owing sponsorship fees and exited alongside fellow mobile phone brand Vivo. The remaining major Chinese sponsors include Lenovo and Hisense, which have title-sponsored the newly added "Referee Cam" and VAR display equipment respectively, as well as Mengniu, which frequently appears with the baffling slogan "Can't drink milk? Try soft milk."

Haaland endorses Wong Lo Kat; Messi's Mengniu ad appears

The time difference of the tournament and China-US relations may have affected Chinese sponsors' appetite, though Chinese companies may have realised that endorsements could yield better results than brand exposure. The heated online discussion over Norwegian striker Haaland's Wong Lo Kat herbal tea advertisement is a case in point. French star Kylian Mbappé endorses "Bu Shui La," an electrolyte drink under Dongpeng Beverage, which was listed prominently in Hong Kong this year, with the ad deliberately aired during the hydration break. Spanish forward Lamine Yamal and Argentine maestro Messi also appear alongside the latter in this edition's Mengniu advertisements. The awkwardness often perceived when world-class footballers endorse products with "Chinese characteristics" is, for Chinese companies, precisely a formula for traffic.

Changes in World Cup sponsors are also reshaping the tournament's form. Although US domestic brands such as Bank of America, telecom company Verizon, and Frito-Lay (parent of Lay's chips) have joined in succession, local host-nation corporate sponsorships often prove short-lived. As for Japanese electronics companies, once regular World Cup sponsors, their fading presence on the pitch has been speculated as a sign of Japan's economic decline — in reality, many have shifted toward the higher-margin commercial market rather than consumer electronics, lacking the incentive to pursue global exposure.

All non-sponsor brands prohibited inside the venues

The sight of Chinese sponsors rallying en masse from the sidelines in recent World Cups may, in the future, be replaced not by another emerging nation but increasingly by ambush marketing lurking outside the venues. Citing the need to protect sponsor interests, FIFA strictly enforces "Clean Stadium" measures, prohibiting all non-sponsor brands inside the grounds. For example, Levi's Stadium, one of this edition's host venues, has been temporarily renamed San Francisco Bay Area Stadium, with the jeans brand's giant in-stadium signage covered in white cloth, while condiment brand logos inside the venue have been taped over with black stickers. Yet brands such as Levi's and Heinz have turned the prohibition into a promotional opportunity. The tight defensive line of FIFA and its sponsors has been picked apart by other brands one by one, forcing a tactical reshuffle.
